text: This closes the course. The capstone asks you to do, once, end to end, on an algorithm of your choosing, everything this course has modeled lesson by lesson: derive it, verify it, and benchmark it honestly.

Pick one algorithm from this course and produce four deliverables. First, a from-scratch derivation in your own words, not copied from the lessons. Second, a small-scale simulation you actually run — 2 or 3 qubits is plenty, and plain matrix code is a fully legitimate choice. Third, at least one independently verified numeric claim, confirmed by actually running your simulation. Fourth, an honest benchmarking section using Lesson 31's checklist and Lesson 33's six-section template.

This course used nothing but plain Node.js matrix arithmetic throughout — the QFT matrix in Chapter 2, phase-estimation probability tables in Chapter 3, Grover's amplitude tables in Chapter 4, and the modular-exponentiation sequences in Chapter 5 were all computed exactly this way. That approach is a fully legitimate model for your own capstone, not a workaround — every number in this entire course was computed before it was written down.

Every chapter made a speedup claim and then immediately qualified it: BQP doesn't contain NP-complete problems in the believed sense, Grover's algorithm gets worse past its optimal iteration count, Shor's algorithm is blocked by hardware, not math. None of those qualifications make the results less real — they make the claims correct. The skill this course has actually been teaching was never just know these six algorithms. It was: compute the real number before you state it, and say precisely what is and isn't true about the result once you have it.

That skill transfers to every future claim about quantum advantage you'll encounter, including the ones made after this course ends — from P versus NP through Shor's algorithm, verified and honestly benchmarked, every step of the way. Congratulations on completing Quantum Algorithms and Complexity Theory.
